input: Draft a personal essay for a grad school application

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Graduate personal essays vary widely — some are 'statement of purpose' focused on academic/research goals, others are 'personal statements' about life experiences. Knowing which type shapes the entire content strategy.
The specific program, field, and school being applied to determines the audience, expected tone, and what the admissions committee values most.
The applicant's background — academic, professional, or personal — is the raw material for the essay. Knowing what experiences are on the table determines what stories can be told.
Most programs specify a strict word or page limit. Knowing this prevents writing something that needs to be drastically cut or padded later.
Personal essays can range from narrative and reflective to analytical and professional in tone. The applicant may have a strong preference or the program may expect a certain style.
The applicant may have a specific weakness in their application (low GPA, gap year, career change) that the essay needs to address, which would completely change the essay's focus.
Knowing the deadline determines urgency and how many drafts/revision rounds are realistic before submission.

gold.taskTitle: Draft a grad school personal essay
gold.taskDescription: Write a compelling personal essay to be submitted as part of a graduate school application.

questions.title: Is this a statement of purpose or a personal statement?
questions.description: Clarify whether the essay should focus on academic/research goals and qualifications (statement of purpose) or on personal narrative and motivations (personal statement), as this determines the entire content structure.

questions.title: What field and type of program are you applying to?
questions.description: Identify the specific academic discipline and degree type (e.g., PhD in Psychology, MBA, MFA in Creative Writing) to tailor the essay's content, vocabulary, and framing to what that admissions committee expects.

questions.title: What key experiences from your background should be highlighted?
questions.description: Gather the most relevant academic, professional, or personal experiences the applicant wants to draw from — research projects, work history, pivotal life events — as these form the essay's core material.

questions.title: What is the required word or page limit for this essay?
questions.description: Establish the hard length constraint set by the program so the draft is scoped correctly from the start and does not require major restructuring later.

questions.title: Should the tone be more narrative and personal, or formal and analytical?
questions.description: Determine the preferred writing style — whether the applicant wants a story-driven, reflective essay or a more structured, professional argument for their candidacy.

questions.title: Is there a weakness in your application this essay needs to address?
questions.description: Find out if there is a specific gap, inconsistency, or red flag in the application (e.g., low GRE scores, a career pivot, a gap year) that the essay should proactively explain or reframe.

questions.title: When is the application deadline for this program?
questions.description: Establish the submission deadline to set a realistic drafting and revision timeline, determining how many rounds of feedback and editing are possible before it must be finalized.
